Figure 31. Speed bin distributions for CE-CERT street sweeper vocation of single-unit short-haul by hour Figure 32 illustrates the speed bin distributions for refuse trucks from the CE-CERT data set. No category had robust data, but urban roads on weekdays had the most logged drive time with up to about 60 hours of data logged for a given hour ID. For urban freeways on weekdays, we see the expected peak around 60 mph for all hours of the day. On urban other roads, we see some higher proportions of driving taking place at 60 mph around midnight; however, for most hours of the day, the proportion of driving time is mostly spent at 5 mph, with steadily decreasing time spent at higher speeds. Rural freeways show some high-speed peaks, and urban freeways on weekends show a diverse spread in peaks by hour of the day, but both categories barely had enough data to be displayed, and thus more fluctuations in distributions are expected but not necessarily representative of real-world driving for these categories. 42 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 33. Speed bin distributions for CE-CERT transit buses by hour For the other bus (airport shuttle in this case) source type from CE-CERT shown in Figure 34, there are only five buses contributing data, leading to choppier distributions in speed. We can pick out a broad 10–20-mph peak for urban other roads and peak around 45–50 mph for urban freeways for most hours of the day. For urban freeways on weekdays, we will show in the average speed section which hours might be more reliable. Based on this analysis, speed distributions from hour IDs 1, 11–13, 17, and 20 could possibly be used and leveraged as a proxy for neighboring hours of the day. On urban other roads on weekdays, just hour IDs 4–6 may need to be replaced by the distributions from hour ID 3 or 7. For urban other roads on weekends, only hour IDs 8, 11, 12, and 14–18 might contain a clearer picture of other bus speeds.
